newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-SECRETIVE FIFA SCORES OWN GOAL.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SECRETIVE FIFA SCORES OWN GOAL.

text.p: World soccer's governing body FIFA met this week to define what constitutes an own goal and promptly scored one itself thanks to its mind-boggling obsession with secrecy.

FIFA could have been preening itself on a spectacular success after persuading South Korea and Japan to overcome apparently irreconcilable differences and agree on crucial decisions about the joint hosting of the 2002 World Cup finals.

Instead, in a naive move which put FIFA in the fourth division as far as public relations are concerned, world soccer leaders attempted an impossible trick -- announcing a major deal had been struck while vowing to keep the details secret for a month.
Predictably, FIFA's bizarrely constructed secret house of cards fell down around its ears within hours
On Wednesday, FIFA invited 120 media representatives to a briefing to tell them that Japan and South Korea had agreed on where the opening match and final of the 2002 World Cup was to be played.
In the next breath, FIFA vice-president Lennart Johansson informed a disbelieving media pack he would not be saying what those decisions were.
The official reason was that the decisions of the World Cup organising committee have to be ratified by the FIFA executive in Barcelona on December 7.
The only thing missing was the Beatles song "Do You Want To Know a Secret?" playing over the speaker system.

"We never said we were going to announce this, that or the other thing," FIFA's communications director Keith Cooper said. "The expectations of the media were excessive in the case of 2002. We're six years out.
"In a normal World Cup, the location of the things like international media centre, the stadium where you're going to play the final aren't fixed that early.
"The Americans didn't decide to play the final in the Rose Bowl six years ahead of the 1994 World Cup, so why the heck should anyone be expecting that kind of information six years ahead this time?
"Anyone who expected all these detailed decisions coming here, frankly hasn't done his homework."

Cooper's remarks failed to address the essential point -- that major decisions had been made and were patently being withheld despite the obvious wide public interest in the world's most popular sporting event
FIFA proved incapable of keeping a secret as the news leaked out within a few hours, first in South Korea, then in Japan.
The next day, when asked to confirm that South Korea would host the opening match and ceremony and Japan the final, FIFA still remained tight-lipped.
"All the participants were unanimous that there should be no information given and that was confirmed twice by Mr Johansson who was chairing the meeting," Cooper said.
"And that's the way it should be simply because the conclusions were to be put to the executive committee and that requires some time. In this case, the next meeting is on December 7."
Johansson's failed attempt to keep the lid on such a seething cauldron will have done him little good in his campaign to unseat Joao Havelange as FIFA president in two years' time.
Not content with one own goal, FIFA managed to score another at Friday's final news conference with its think tank, Task Force 2000.

The annual meeting, which brought together some of soccer's biggest personalities and brightest minds, including Johan Cruyff, Michel Platini and Franz Beckenbauer, discussed many of the pressing issues in the game like the golden goal rule, time-outs and two referees -- all before lunch.
By the time the media arrived for the scheduled press conference the Task Force had already left.
"It was decided late last night to start the meeting at eight instead of nine because the chairman Lennart Johansson had another pressing meeting," Cooper said.
